title: Trust Signals Workbook — Messaging for Degradation & Fallbacks
content:
Purpose:
This workbook captures GTM copy, competitive notes and recommended incident narratives for situations when inference quality, latency or capacity degrade. It is a working doc — want quick scripts for marketing, in-product banners, AM talking points, and A/B test ideas for language that preserves trust.

Audience:
- Sales and AE (enterprise talking points)
- Customer success (incident scripts, SLAs)
- Product marketing (site messaging and FAQ)
- Developer docs and SDK team (error semantics)

High-level framing (3 trust pillars to emphasize)
1) Transparency — tell customers what happened, impact, and next steps. Avoid euphemisms.
2) Predictability — explain fallback behavior and how apps will behave (model swap, reduced throughput, increased latency).
3) Control — describe what customers can configure (pin model versions, routing policies, capacity tiers).

Messaging taxonomy (severity-driven):
- Info (no user impact): "Heads-up: scheduled model redistribution to improve throughput — no change to responses."
- Degraded (reduced perf/throughput or quality): "We’re seeing elevated latency and may route some requests to a lower-latency model variant. Your API will continue to respond; you may see slightly concise outputs. We’ll restore the usual model shortly."
- Partial outage (significant degradation): "We’re experiencing elevated error rates in region us-west-2. We’re routing traffic to alternate region(s) for continued availability; you may see increased latency. Engineering is on it; ETA 30–90 mins."
- Major outage (widespread failure): "Service interruption in multiple regions. We’ve activated fallbacks: best-effort responses from cached outputs and compact model variants. Prioritizing high-value traffic. Status page updated every 15 minutes."

Fallback taxonomy (technical -> plain-language mapping):
- Model-fallback (technical): route to a smaller/quantized model variant
  - Plain: "Switching to a faster, slightly smaller model to keep responses flowing."
- Region-fallback: route to another region/replica
  - Plain: "Routing your requests to a nearby healthy region — you may see a small latency change."
- Cached-response fallback: serve cached completions for repeated prompts
  - Plain: "Delivering previously validated answers for repeat queries to reduce delay."
- Degraded feature mode: disable expensive features (tools, function-calls, streaming)
  - Plain: "Temporarily disabling advanced features to keep core responses reliable."

Recommended in-product microcopy (variants to A/B test):
A (empathetic + specific): "We detected a service disruption affecting generation speed. We're switching to a faster model variant in the background so your app keeps working. Expect slightly shorter responses until we restore normal capacity."
B (concise + action oriented): "Temporary performance degradation. Auto-fallback active. No action required; restore in progress."
C (for enterprise tenants with dedicated capacity): "Your reserved pool is operating under elevated load. We’ve prioritized your critical routes and opened additional burst capacity per your SLA."

Customer email / support templates (short):
- Subject: "Update: Temporary changes to model routing (us-west-2)"
- Body (opening): "Hi <Customer>, we want to keep you informed: between 11:02–11:40 UTC we observed increased errors in us-west-2. To avoid interruption, we routed traffic to a compatible model in eu-west-1. You may notice slightly higher latency. No action required; we'll revert once the region stabilizes."
- Closing: "If you prefer we pin your traffic to a single region or disable auto-fallbacks, reply and we’ll assist. For critical customers we can enable dedicated capacity."

Sales / AE positioning bullets (competitive differentiators to use during calls):
- Unlike many hosted APIs, our platform exposes the fallback policy and lets you opt-in/out per route.
- We surface the exact model variant used per request so you can audit quality regressions.
- Multi-region routing is automatic with tuning knobs: your team can prioritize latency vs cost.
- For Dedicated/Private customers we support SLA-backed reserved pools and predictable failover behavior.

Quick competitor notes (raw, working scan):
- CloudAI provider — typically fails closed or returns 5xx without transparent fallback; can be combined messaging: highlights add little on observability.
- LLM-API competitor — offers single-model primary fallback to smaller models but does not surface per-request model identity; hard to debug regressions.
- Inference runtime vendor (self-host) — customers get control but must build routing/rollout tooling; long tail of custom ops.
How Redwood leans into these gaps:
- Emphasize transparent per-request model identity and cost/latency tradeoffs in docs and UI.
- Sell the ops+runtime combo: you get runtime guarantees plus console/traceability.

Incident narrative playbook (for CS + comms):
1) T+0 (detection): short internal alert — include scope (routes, regions), observed symptoms (5xx, p95 spike), initial mitigation (auto-fallback, capacity bump).
2) T+5 (initial customer touch): publish a short status page note and targeted emails to affected customers using templated language above.
3) T+15 (engineer update): explain root-cause hypothesis, mitigation, and ETA. Use plain language + bullet list of affected features.
4) T+resolution: detailed postmortem sent to impacted customers summarizing cause, mitigation, and permanent fixes/roadmap items. Offer remediation (credits, free dedicated capacity trial) as appropriate.

What to include in customer postmortems (customer-facing summary):
- Impact window (start/end), affected routes/regions, observable customer impact (error rate, latency delta), cause (short, clear), actions taken, and timeline of key events.
- Remediation steps and timeline for permanent mitigation.
- Specific next steps for customers who want additional protections (how to enable regional pin, dedicated capacity).

Metrics and signals to communicate (make these digestible):
- Visible: p95 latency delta (ms), error rate (% of requests), percent of traffic auto-routed, percent of requests served by fallback variant.
- Business: percent of API calls failed for top-10 customers, impact on SLA met/unmet, churn risk indicators.

Testing & experiments (quick ideas):
- A/B test banner copy: empathetic vs transactional vs technical. Measure NPS/CSAT of the notice.
- Drill: run scheduled simulated fallback (internal customers) and measure comprehension of message and support load.
- Opt-in telemetry: show customers a replay of the exact request path (region/model variant) for a sample request; measure helpdesk volume reduction.

In-product UX recommendations (ops -> PM handoff):
- Add a per-route toggle: auto-fallback (on/off) + fallback policy (prefer-latency, prefer-cost, prefer-quality).
- Expose the last-known model id & region on every API response header and in the Console request log.
- Status panel: small timeline widget showing last 24h degrade events and what fallback was used.

Sample incident scripts for AM / CS (role-playable):
- AM: "We saw your calls routed to a compact model briefly. You might notice slightly shorter completions — we can whitelist sample prompts for higher-fidelity processing or schedule a dedicated capacity trial."
- CS: "I know this impacts your product. We routed you to a cached best-effort while the region recovered. I can share the postmortem and help apply mitigation rules for high-priority routes."

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Do we publish default fallback policies in the public docs or behind an enterprise gate? (recommendation: public, but advanced controls documented for Enterprise)
- What is the standard customer credit policy for degradation events? (ops + finance decision)
- Should we surface instance-level telemetry by default or require opt-in for data sensitivity?

Next steps (owner + timeline):
- PM (Meera) to draft Console UI copy for fallback toggles — due 2026-02-28.
- Docs (Jonah) to create a public FAQ: "How Redwood keeps your app online" — due 2026-03-10.
- GTM (Aisha) to prepare 3 email templates and 4 in-product banner variants for A/B test — draft by 2026-03-01.

Notes to self / rough fragments:
- Keep language active ("we routed" vs "we may route").
- Avoid technical jargon in customer_comm emails; include a TL;DR at top.
- For enterprise sales decks, include a small chart showing "mean recovery time with Redwood routing vs typical provider" (internal metric).

End of workbook — use this as canonical source for banner copy tests and incident templates. Update linked_artifacts when PM/Docs PRs land.
